title: Hitting Set conjecture
formal:
Is the randomized Hitting Set conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(c\ge1\) such that no uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm decides the following problem in worst-case time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)? The input is two lists \(A,B\), each of \(n\) subsets of \([d]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\). Decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \forall b\in B:\quad a\cap b\ne\varnothing.\]
The chosen set must be one of the supplied sets in \(A\). This is the source's fine-grained two-list problem, not the general optimization problem of selecting a small hitting set from the universe.
why: This hypothesis captures a quadratic barrier with an existential choice followed by a universal test. It supports fine-grained lower bounds for graph radius, centers and quantified geometric problems where the more familiar two-existential-quantifier orthogonal-vectors hypothesis does not directly match the task. Settling it would clarify the role of quantifier order in fine-grained complexity.
status_note: The original 2016 conjecture and the 2021 logarithmic-dimension formulation were checked on 2026-09-14. A bounded later search, including 2026 graph-center work, found continuing conditional applications and no resolution of the selected randomized bounded-error hypothesis.

sentences: Two lists contain subsets of a logarithmic-size universe.
The task is to find whether one supplied set in the first list intersects every set in the second.
The conjecture rules out a single fixed polynomial improvement over quadratic time across all constant multiples of logarithmic dimension.
The selected model permits randomization with bounded error and counts all word-RAM computation.
Its existential–universal structure makes it useful for graph-radius and quantified-ordering lower bounds.

definitions:
Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Sets are supplied explicitly as \(d\)-bit incidence vectors; lists may contain repetitions and empty sets. Equivalently, the answer is yes if some vector \(a\in A\) has integer inner product \(\sum_{j=1}^d a_j b_j>0\) with every \(b\in B\). The coordinate sum is over integers, not modulo two. The dimension constant \(c\) is fixed independently of input size.

Use a word RAM with word length
\[
w=\max\!\left\{\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\rceil,\ \lceil\log_2(2nd+n+d+8)\rceil\right\}.
\]
The second term ensures that the full explicit input and its headers fit in the address universe even for small \(n\) and a large fixed dimension constant \(c\). For every fixed \(c\), it is eventually dominated by the first term, so this finite-input correction leaves the stated asymptotic time hypothesis unchanged. Incidence vectors are packed into consecutive words, with unused bits zero. A machine has a finite program independent of \(n\), word-addressed memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, copies, comparisons, branches, arithmetic addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero; division by zero may return zero. A uniformly random independent \(w\)-bit word is available at unit cost. Memory initially contains only the instance; any further preprocessing or lookup-table construction is charged. There are no oracles, advice or unit-cost operations on arbitrarily long integers.

A bounded-error algorithm must output the correct yes/no answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input. Its runtime bound applies to every random tape and every input, not only in expectation. For fixed \(\varepsilon,c\), a forbidden algorithm would have constants \(K,n_0\) such that it takes at most \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\) instructions for every \(n\ge n_0\); the constants and program may depend on \(c,\varepsilon\). Finite smaller instances must also be decided correctly within finite time.

The order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) is essential. Refutation requires one \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every fixed \(c\) there is an algorithm with that same exponent saving; it does not require the same program or multiplicative constant for all \(c\). Conversely, a faster algorithm at one small dimension constant does not refute the conjecture. Choosing integral \(c\) is harmless because extra zero coordinates pad smaller dimensions.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated bounded-error word-RAM model. A refutation must supply a common positive exponent saving across all fixed dimension constants. A proof conditional on another unproved hypothesis is not a proof of this conjecture. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a restricted instruction set, or an isolated value of \(c\) does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: For fixed \(c\), comparing every pair of packed vectors gives an \(O(cn^2)\)-time baseline. The conjecture permits savings that vanish as dimension grows; it rules out one fixed polynomial saving valid across all dimension constants.

Orthogonal Vectors asks whether some pair has zero inner product. Here one supplied vector must have nonzero inner product with every vector on the other side. Exchanging these quantifiers changes the question, just as finding a graph center differs from finding a distant pair of vertices.

The 2021 source transfers this hypothesis to model checking with an existential–universal–existential quantifier pattern. Such reductions establish consequences of the conjecture, not an unconditional lower bound for Hitting Set.

The card retains the randomized bounded-error convention of the saved formulation and specifies its machine model. Restricted-dimensional algorithms and expected-time-only guarantees should be compared against these exact quantifiers and resources.
